title: Make AX hold 42
summary: Start with one instruction and find the operand hiding beside its opcode.
goal: Halt with AX = 42.
hints: The first byte B8 selects AX. Leave that opcode alone.
The next two bytes form the immediate value, low byte first.
42 in decimal is 00101010 in eight binary digits.
explanation: MOV does not calculate: it copies the immediate into AX. The low operand byte changes from 41 to 42 while the high byte stays zero.

startAnnotations.explanation: Mask interrupts so the final halt stays stopped.

Stop with the current register value.

title: Borrow below zero
summary: Unsigned subtraction can wrap even when the stored result looks large.
goal: Halt with AX = 0xFFFF, CF = 1 and ZF = 0.
hints: The SUB immediate is already one. Change the initial AX value.

Start from zero: 0 − 1 wraps to FFFF.
explanation: Sixteen result bits cannot store negative one as an unsigned value. They wrap to FFFF; CF records the borrow separately. ZF stays clear because FFFF is not zero.

startAnnotations.explanation: Keep the final halt stopped.

explanation: CMP performs a subtraction only to set flags. Equal values set ZF, so JZ takes its +3 displacement from the end of the jump to HLT. AX remains 42.

title: Escape the infinite jump
summary: A negative displacement sends the instruction pointer back to the same opcode.
goal: Reach HLT within 96 model steps.
hints: EB is a short unconditional jump. Its operand is a signed eight-bit displacement.
FE represents −2, measured from the end of the two-byte instruction.
A displacement of zero lands on the next instruction, HLT.
explanation: The starting jump ends at offset 3, then subtracts two to return to offset 1. Changing FE to 00 breaks that cycle. The bounded validator rejects the endless starting loop.

00110001 11000000 # instruction | XOR AX,AX | 31 /r; ModR/M C0 = register AX XOR register AX, producing zero.
10001110 11011000 # instruction | MOV DS,AX | 8E /r; D8 selects DS and AX; data addresses use segment zero.
10001110 11000000 # instruction | MOV ES,AX | 8E /r; C0 selects ES and AX.
10001110 11010000 # instruction | MOV SS,AX | 8E /r; D0 selects SS and AX; stack segment becomes zero.
10111100 00000000 01111100 # instruction | MOV SP,7C00 | BC = B8+SP; little-endian 7C00 places stack below the loaded sector.
11111100 # instruction | CLD | FC clears direction flag; LODSB advances SI.
11111011 # instruction | STI | FB enables BIOS keyboard/timer interrupts after stack is ready.

01000010 # instruction | INC DX | 42 = 40+DX; selects divisor high-byte port.

10110000 00000011 # instruction | MOV AL,03 | B0 selects 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit; clears DLAB.
11101110 # instruction | OUT DX,AL | EE writes 8N1 UART configuration.

title: Clear two registers in fewer bytes
summary: Two immediate loads reach the goal. Replace their tail with a smaller literal program.
goal: Preserve the seven setup bytes, halt with AX = BX = 0 and SP = 7C00, using at most 12 payload bytes.
hints: The locked setup gives AX and BX different nonzero values; clearing cannot rely on initial zeros.
XOR of a register with itself takes two bytes. MOV immediate takes three.
31 C0 clears AX. Clear BX with 31 DB, or copy AX into BX with 89 C3. Keep the final F4.
explanation: Both reviewed twelve-byte programs save two bytes from the fourteen-byte starting program. Two self-XOR instructions and XOR followed by MOV reach the same register and stack goals. Arithmetic flags are deliberately outside this challenge's goals; clearing with XOR does not preserve the flags of MOV immediate.
visual: 14 → 12 payload bytes · two XORs or XOR + register MOV · flags outside the goal

title: Reuse a value, save one byte
summary: AX already holds forty-two. Avoid spelling the same immediate again when setting BX.
goal: Preserve the seven setup bytes, halt with AX = BX = 42 and SP = 7C00, using at most 10 payload bytes.
hints: The locked setup establishes AX = 42 and gives BX a different value.
A register MOV uses two bytes. PUSH AX followed by POP BX uses one byte each.
Try 89 C3 F4 or 50 5B F4 after the setup. The stack pair must restore SP.
explanation: Both ten-byte programs save one byte from the eleven-byte starting program. Register MOV copies AX directly. PUSH/POP transfers through the established stack and balances SP, but leaves 2A 00 in stack RAM. The goals require register values, halt and balanced SP; they do not require untouched stack memory or prove one version faster.
visual: 11 → 10 payload bytes · MOV register or PUSH/POP · balanced SP, distinct RAM effects
